claims.text: The starting alloy is additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3.
The as-built alloy has a predominantly fcc matrix.
The starting alloy has notable strength and fatigue performance.
Degradation during elevated-temperature gas exposure is governed primarily by synergistic effects of Al, Cr, and Ti on surface-oxide formation, stability, and protectiveness.
Competitive oxidation kinetics determine the alloy's resistance to degradation.
Phase readjustment at the matrix/oxide interface influences degradation resistance.
The fcc matrix remains intact unless significant elemental depletion or phase transformation occurs.
Al, Cr, and Ti compete to form Al2O3, Cr2O3, and TiO2, respectively.
Synergistic interactions among Al, Cr, and Ti in the high-entropy matrix alter oxide-scale kinetics and stability.
Limited elemental depletion together with fcc-matrix stability promotes protective scale formation and minimizes degradation.
Near-surface phase readjustment or significant elemental depletion promotes non-protective oxides or matrix destabilization and accelerates degradation.
Oxidizing-gas exposure at 700–1000°C will produce complex multicomponent scales dominated by Al, Cr, and Ti oxides.
Substantial near-surface depletion of Al, Cr, or Ti can cause local phase transformation or loss of mechanical integrity.
Reducing gases will suppress oxide formation relative to oxidizing gases.
Reducing-gas exposure may induce elemental segregation or phase changes if the matrix becomes destabilized.
The as-built baseline has no surface oxide scale.
The as-built baseline has a uniform elemental distribution.
The proposed mechanism applies to similarly composed fcc alloys exposed to oxidizing or reducing atmospheres at 700–1000°C.
